x: Several of our "Juniors" ran well, including Button, Tom Pritchard, Davis, Field and others. A new member, Robertshaw, is promising and will do much better. We were pleased to see Button with us as he will soon be off to Australia.
Pritchard is to be congratulated on his excellent running and one of our new men, Robertshaw, shewed up very promisingly.
After the first circuit of the country, the above-named was still first of our men, with Robertshaw just behind. As the latter was in the "B" team this was not too promising, for St.
Every man ran well—Robertshaw particularly to finish 10th, and had the going been heavier I fancy he would have troubled the leaders. His is the best performance by any member of ours since the war.

Robertshaw, whose fine performance in the South of the Thames race was still fresh in our minds, was obliged to retire from the race owing to an injury to his back sustained when clambering over a stile.

…to the slaughter on the journey to Leamington to run against the "Stagbearers," and we had an early disappointment, for Robertshaw missed the train and so nearly did our treasurer who, waiting until the last minute, just managed to get on board with the help of the Guard as the train was moving out…

Robertshaw now had the difficult task of negotiating Redhill and the switchback course as far as Horley. This was a lengthy stretch of over 6 miles, and it speaks well for his pluck that despite a "bad time" he gave a creditable display and only surrendered two places.

Robertshaw, perhaps our most successful runner last winter, was only nineteenth. He is not yet fit, which is all to the good, for he is not likely to become stale at the time of our more important races next February and March.

S Webb and Robertshaw Down Gravelly Hill and along the Horse-ride to the Flagstaff, thence to the Windmill and the Village, which marked the end of the first lap, the course continued, and at the latter point Duffett and Rice turned together, with Allum but a yard behind .
Webb were unable to run owing to foot trouble, and Robertshaw was forced to retire from the race when well placed, owing to a recurrence of ankle strain.
Then came Penny (8th), Allum (13th), Webb (25th), Robertshaw (26th), Khlopin (29th), Smith (44th), O'Kell, who had come from Stoke to help in the good work (48th), Rice (52nd), Jones, A.

Allum, Webb and Rice came along together some distance behind, and Robertshaw came later, looking none too comfortable. A mile later it looked as if Mitchell would catch Penny, for he was running very easily and had picked up several places.
…runners in the following order: Cohen, Allum, Penny, Jack Flower, Frank Webb, Nuti (T.V.H.), Carter, Dewberry, Morrell, Robertshaw, Smith and Joe Flower.…

No, only Robertshaw, with Bill Webb loping along after him, looking as though it was "too much fag" even to run. At this point about two miles from the start, the issue seemed already to be between the two in the lead, with Jack Flower standing an outside chance of getting on terms.
Frank Webb did some very fast running in the last two miles for he was hung up for a long time by barbed wire. This misfortune happened to Robertshaw, and J.
Webb, Robertshaw and Mains. The furlong junior championship was a tragedy.

From this relay to the end the Club were supreme, going further ahead at each stage; Dewberry, Joe and Jack Flower and Robertshaw, in the order, all running their course in fine style, Jack Flower doing third fastest time for us.
Carter and Robertshaw soon took the lead, which they retained to the finish. The course proved to be a sporting one with plenty of mud and water, and we managed to run out winners.

The other members of our team, omitting Allum and Robertshaw, both of whom retired through indisposition, packed much too far back for a forward position to be gained, but even so we were the third Southern club to finish and reversed our placings with Enfield A.C.
Robertshaw's machine would not function properly, however, and Wally Bayliss saved us by finding some of his old dash and finishing eighth. This enabled us to beat Epsom by three points.
Carter, Robertshaw and others were well up. Out into the country and Arthur Penny thought it was time to get going, so he went into the lead unchallenged.

Leaving my vantage point I hastened down to below the golf-links to see field go "out" for the second time, and although the leaders had gone away by the time I had got there, it was some consolation to see that Walker and Robertshaw had moved up, after both having experienced a bad patch.

They were, however, closely followed by Robertshaw, Mitchell and Cecil Penny. At 3 miles Penny was 100 yards in front of Weatherill, and Footer had come up to 3rd place, about 80 yards behind Weatherill Both Carter and Abberton were running well and each had picked up a place.
The following season, 1932, we experienced a minor set-back and were placed fourth, our score being 169 points. Our scoring men were Footer 3, Flower 11, Allum 24, Robertshaw 35, Duffett 44, W.
